passage:
Yamini, you asked about my favourite singer, so here goes. I’m Disha, and I was fifteen, and I’d played her album every night for two years. Last month a report said she had treated her staff badly for a long time and hidden it.
First I refused to read it. Then I read it and felt sick. I didn’t delete the songs, because a couple of them got me through exams. But I stopped posting her lyrics.
When my friends said, “People exaggerate,” I said, “The songs are still good, and what she did is still wrong.” Nobody answered. Holding both things feels strange, but pretending felt worse.

qa.q: How old was Disha when the album played every night?
qa.a: Disha was fifteen and had played the album every night for two years.

qa.q: What was Disha feeling after reading the report?
qa.a: Disha felt sick and deeply disappointed after reading it, which shows how much the singer had meant to Disha.

qa.q: What choice did Disha make about the songs, and why did it work?
qa.a: Disha kept the songs but stopped posting the lyrics. That kept what was good in the music without excusing what the singer did.

qa.q: What might Disha's friends who said people exaggerate have been feeling?
qa.a: They may have been trying to protect their own admiration, or avoiding the discomfort of the report. Their silence after Disha's answer suggests they had no ready reply.

grounding: Shows a teenager working through disappointment in an admired singer, keeping the music without excusing the wrongdoing.

passage:
Kishore had a poster of an actor above his desk. When news broke that the actor had shouted at junior crew members and then apologised in a half-hearted way, Kishore stared at the poster for a long time. I’m Karthik, his classmate, and I was next to him.
Manoj said, “So what? Everyone does that.” Kishore said, “Not everyone.” Ayesha stayed silent and looked at her notebook.
That evening Kishore said, “I still like the films. What he did to those people isn’t okay, and I’m not going to pretend it is.” He took the poster down and slid it inside his cupboard door. I couldn’t tell whether he felt sad or angry.

qa.q: What did the actor do that upset Kishore?
qa.a: The actor shouted at junior crew members and then apologised in a half-hearted way.

qa.q: What might Kishore have been feeling as he stared at the poster?
qa.a: Kishore was probably disappointed, since the actor had been someone he admired. Karthik could not tell if it was sadness or anger, so both are possible.

qa.q: Which choice of Kishore's showed he could keep the good and still be honest?
qa.a: He said he still liked the films but refused to pretend the behaviour was fine. He then took the poster down rather than arguing about it.

qa.q: How might Ayesha, who stayed silent, have seen the exchange between Manoj and Kishore?
qa.a: Ayesha may have agreed with Kishore but felt it was hard to speak against Manoj, or she may have been unsure. Looking at her notebook shows she stayed out of it.

grounding: Shows a teenager, seen by a classmate, working through disappointment in an admired actor without excusing the behaviour.

passage: Tuesday: the news broke that Karan Mehta, the fast bowler on Anirban's bedroom poster, had been banned for tampering with the ball. Anirban read it three times. 'It's fake,' he told Yash at school. Yash showed him the video. Anirban went quiet and didn't eat his tiffin. Friday: the other boys were mocking Karan Mehta, calling him a cheat. Anirban wanted to defend him, then didn't. He felt stupid for having loved him. Two weeks later, Sunday: Anirban took the poster down. He kept the notebook where he'd copied Karan's run-up drills, though. At practice he told Yash, 'The run-up was still good. The cheating was still wrong. Both.' Yash nodded. 'Both.'

qa.q: Why was Karan Mehta banned?
qa.a: For tampering with the ball.

qa.q: How did Anirban feel on Friday when the boys mocked Karan Mehta?
qa.a: He felt torn and embarrassed, wanting to defend his idol but feeling stupid for having loved him.

qa.q: Which choice showed Anirban handling the disappointment maturely?
qa.a: Taking the poster down but keeping the run-up drills, saying the skill was good and the cheating wrong.

qa.q: How might Yash have seen Anirban's change over the two weeks?
qa.a: Yash watched Anirban move from denial to acceptance and seems to respect the 'both' answer.

grounding: Over two weeks a teenager works through an idol's wrongdoing, keeping what was good without excusing it.

passage: Seema, you're upset your favourite singer said those ugly things? Your Thomas appachan had a hero too. In 1972, in Kochi, it was Joseph Ittiyavira, the best striker in our district. I copied his hairstyle, his celebrations, even the way he tied his laces. Then the newspaper said he'd taken money to lose a match. I was sixteen. I cried, then shouted that it was lies. My father sat with me and said, 'He can be a great player and have done a wrong thing. You don't have to pick one.' It took me months. I stopped defending him. But I kept practising his left-foot shot, because that was mine now, not his. I'm still good with my left foot.

qa.q: What was Joseph Ittiyavira accused of?
qa.a: Taking money to lose a match.

qa.q: How did sixteen-year-old Thomas feel when he read the newspaper?
qa.a: Heartbroken and angry, crying and then insisting it was lies.

qa.q: What choice in the story helped young Thomas move forward?
qa.a: His father's words that a great player can do a wrong thing, which let Thomas stop defending the striker while keeping the left-foot shot as his own.

qa.q: What might Thomas's father have been hoping when he sat with him?
qa.a: To help his son grieve the hero without losing his love of football or his sense of right and wrong.

grounding: A grandfather recalls working through a teenage hero's wrongdoing, keeping the good without excusing the wrong.

passage: Hansa's school presentation on her favourite author, Meera Sabnis, was due at nine the next morning. At eleven at night, Irawati sent her a link: several of Sabnis's former assistants said she had bullied them for years, with messages as proof. Hansa sat on her bed, slides open, feeling sick. She had quoted Sabnis on kindness on slide three. Part of her wanted to pretend she hadn't seen it. Part of her wanted to delete everything. She called Irawati. 'Her books still helped me. But what she did is real.' They talked till one. In the morning, Hansa presented the books and added one new slide: 'The author has been accused of bullying her staff. I still value these stories, but I don't excuse that.' Her teacher nodded slowly.

qa.q: Who did Sabnis's former assistants say she had bullied?
qa.a: The assistants themselves, for years.

qa.q: What was Hansa feeling at eleven at night with her slides open?
qa.a: She felt sick and torn between pretending she hadn't seen it and deleting everything.

qa.q: How did Hansa handle the presentation, and why was it mature?
qa.a: She kept what was good in the books but added a slide naming the accusations and saying she doesn't excuse them.

qa.q: How might Hansa's teacher see the new slide?
qa.a: The teacher's slow nod suggests respect for Hansa's honesty in holding both truths.

grounding: Under deadline pressure, a teenager works through an admired author's wrongdoing and keeps the good without excusing it.

passage: The news broke on a Tuesday: the author of Simran's favourite fantasy series had been sending cruel messages to young writers for years, and three of them had shared screenshots. By lunch her class at the Lucknow school had split. Kritika said, "Cancel him, burn the books." Farhan said, "It's fake, it must be." Simran said nothing. At home she took the seven books off her shelf and sat on the floor with them. Those stories had got her through Class 7. Her older sister Preeti knocked. "You okay?" "I don't know what to do with them." "You don't have to decide tonight." Simran thought for a long while. "The books helped me. What he did hurt real people. Both are true." She put the books in a box, not the bin, and wrote the three writers' names in her notebook to look up their work.

qa.q: How many books did Simran take off her shelf?
qa.a: She took the seven books off her shelf.

qa.q: What was Simran feeling as she sat on the floor with the books?
qa.a: She felt disappointed and torn, because the stories had helped her but the author had hurt real people.

qa.q: Which of Simran's choices was balanced, and why?
qa.a: Boxing the books instead of binning or defending them, and looking up the three writers, kept what helped her without excusing the behaviour.

qa.q: Why might Kritika and Farhan have reacted so differently?
qa.a: Kritika's anger and Farhan's denial may both come from the same shock at a trusted author, handled in opposite ways.

grounding: Shows a teenager working through disappointment in an admired author, keeping what was good in the work without excusing the behaviour.
